messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 62
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bank Teller
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 58

He still sees the bank’s fluorescent lights flicker, but now the hum sounds like the grinding of metal. It was eight months ago—a Tuesday, just before noon. The vault’s security door had jammed during a routine maintenance check, and his manager, Frank, asked for help sliding it back onto its track. John, a teller for thirty-two years, knew the door’s weight. They braced together, counted to three, and heaved. The door lurched sideways, its upper hinge shearing free. John lost his grip. The door swung hard and caught Frank across the temple, driving him to the marble floor. Blood pooled beneath Frank’s head before anyone could shout.

John held a towel to the wound, his hands stained, while someone called 911. Frank survived, but the brain injury left him with a permanent limp, garbled speech, and a memory that stops at the morning of that day. John visits him once, at the rehabilitation center. Frank doesn’t recognize him. John hasn’t gone back.

Now, every time John slides open a cash drawer, his right hand tingles. He hears the *thunk* of steel on bone. Sometimes, during a silent moment between customers, the sound runs through his head in a loop, and he feels the towel turn slick and warm again. He blinks hard, forces his eyes to the numbers on the screen. He has started mis-sorting bills, once handing a customer an extra hundred. His supervisor pulled him aside, friendly but concerned. “You alright, John? You seem off.” John nodded and said he hadn’t been sleeping well. That part was true.

He wakes most nights around 3 a.m., heart hammering, from a dream where the door falls not on Frank but on his wife, Susan. He sits up in the dark, breath shallow, and waits for the dread to ebb. Susan stirs, asks if he’s okay. He says it’s nothing, rolls away. He cannot tell her the real nightmare—the one where Frank’s eyes go glassy and John just stands there, frozen, watching. He wakes from that one shaking, sometimes crying, though he hasn’t cried in front of her since their son’s wedding.

At work, John avoids the south hallway where the vault is. He takes the long route through the break room to reach the restroom. When a customer drops a heavy coin purse, John flinches so hard he nearly knocks over his coffee cup. His fingers curl into fists. He feels his face flush, and he excuses himself to the back, standing alone by the industrial sink, staring at the grout between the tiles. He tells himself it was an accident, that any of them could have lost their grip. But the thought slides away, replaced by the image of Frank’s body on the floor, the metallic smell of blood, the way the ambulance lights painted the lobby red.

He used to enjoy the small talk with regulars—the ones who call him “Mr. T,” ask about his grandkids. Now he smiles mechanically, counts out their cash, and hopes they don’t linger. When Susan suggests they host the annual holiday party this year, John says he’s too tired. He stops joining the Friday poker game at the community center; the laughter feels like static. He spends evenings on the back porch, watching cars pass, replaying that Tuesday.

Last week, while driving to the grocery store, he saw a man in a blue jacket that looked like the uniform Frank wore. John’s foot slammed the brake, and the car behind him honked. He pulled into a parking lot, hands trembling, and sat there for ten minutes, unable to turn the wheel. He told Susan it was bumper-to-bumper traffic.

The bank manager schedules a meeting for next Thursday. John suspects it is about the counting errors. He already knows he will apologize, promise to do better, and then come home, sit on the porch, and wait for the night to fall. He cannot imagine a future where the sound of that door stopped following him.
